A unified convergence theory for adaptive first-order
methods in the nonconvex case, including AdaNorm,
full and diagonal AdaGrad, Shampoo and Muon

S. Gratton  and Ph. L. Toint ††thanks: Université de Toulouse, INP, IRIT, Toulouse, France. Email: serge.gratton@enseeiht.fr. Work partially supported by 3IA Artificial and Natural Intelligence Toulouse Institute (ANITI), French ”Investing for the Future - PIA3” program under the Grant agreement ANR-19-PI3A-0004”††thanks: Université de Toulouse, INP, IRIT, Toulouse, France, and NAXYS, University of Namur, Namur, Belgium. Email: philippe.toint@unamur.be
16 IV 2026
Abstract

A unified framework for first-order optimization algorithms for nonconvex unconstrained optimization is proposed that uses adaptively preconditioned gradients and includes popular methods such as full and diagonal AdaGrad, AdaNorm, as well as adpative variants of Shampoo and Muon. This framework also allows combining heterogeneous geometries across different groups of variables while preserving a unified convergence analysis. A fully stochastic global rate-of-convergence analysis is conducted for all methods in the framework, with and without two types of momentum, using reasonable assumptions on the variance of the gradient oracle and without assuming bounded stochastic gradients or small enough stepsize.

Keywords: Unconstrained nonconvex optimization, first-order methods, global rate of convergence, Adam, AdaGrad, Shampoo, Muon.

1 Introduction

We consider the problem of finding a first-order critical point for the optimization problem

minX⁡𝔼⁡[f⁡(X,ξ)]\min_{X}\mathbb{E}\!\left[f(X,\xi)\right] (1.1)

where ff is a smooth, possibly nonconvex function of XX and ξ\xi is a suitably defined random variable. Stochastic first-order methods for solving problem (1.1) have surged as a major research theme in recent years, essentially motivated by their very successful use in deep learning applications [11]. Because most of these methods do not evaluate the objective function at all11 1 They belong to the Objective-Function-Free Optimization (OFFO) class., they are very robust in the presence of stochastic noise, a crucial feature in these applications. Starting with stochastic gradient descent [43], this domain has seen major advances in the last twenty years, with landmark proposals such as AdaNorm [45, 15, 51], AdaGrad [15, 39], Adam [30], and, more recently, Shampoo [25] and Muon [28]. The number of their variants (see [46, 40, 52, 51, 4, 48, 44] to cite only a few examples) has grown to such a number that a decent review is today a major undertaking (and beyond the scope of this paper). Their convergence analysis has followed the same trend, with significant contributions in particular in [58, 42, 52, 34, 14, 23, 18, 29, 21, 17, 36, 49, 26, 27, 57, 33, 35, 41].

A major theme in this domain has been preconditioning, as a cure to the known sensitivity of pure gradient methods to (even modest) problem ill-conditioning. The AdaGrad adaptive diagonal preconditioning strategy proposed in [45, 15] and used in Adam [30], has been at the source of many of the proposals mentioned above, first for unstructured methods (e.g. [52, 21, 1, 2]) and, in the past few years, for methods exploiting the tensor structure of deep-learning applications [48, 35, 44, 56]. The convergence of many of these methods has been investigated, but is often specific to the method considered. From our point of view, notable exceptions are [24] whose interesting interpretation of preconditioning in dual norms covers AdaGrad and some variants in the convex case, [14] covering both Adam and AdaGrad in the nonconvex case, [21] covering AdaGrad and divergent series variants in the nonconvex case, [54, 31] covering AdaGrad, AdaNorm and Shampoo in the convex case, and [41] where the idea of preconditioning in dual norm is applied to discuss (non-adaptive) variants of Muon in the nonconvex case.

As it turns out, results for methods for nonconvex problems involving momentum either conclude to non-convergence [47] or to convergence to a mere neighbourhood of a critical point [14], or assume either that gradients are uniformly bounded [42] or (somewhat unrealistically) that the user specifies a stepsize parameter that is sufficiently small compared to the inverse of the problem’s Lipschitz constant [23, 26, 53], or to the termination criterion [32, 57].

As far as the authors are aware, the convergence theory for all these proposals (except [54] in the convex case) consider that the parameters to optimize are of a single type, either a vector of scalars, or a matrix, each having its own dedicated preconditioner. However, practical applications often mix those types (for instance considering together activation levels and biases, and weight matrices in neural networks). For instance, Shampoo-type methods are typically applied at the level of individual matrix blocks, rather than globally across all parameters, due to their computational cost [3]. Structured second-order methods such as K-FAC [38] approximate curvature information using block-wise Kronecker factorizations, and these methods are typically applied only to selected layers, while simpler and less costly updates are used elsewhere. This practice is for instance recommended in [55, 20, 41, 8], although without analysis for adaptive methods. It is therefore interesting to consider the space of variables as the product space of blocks of parameters of possibly different types. In particular, this has the advantage of allowing a unified view of both vectors and matrix parameters.

Our paper attempts to exploit this observation to derive a general theory. Its main contributions are the following.

  1. 1.

    It provides the first (to the authors’ knowldedge) truly unified convergence analysis of adaptive preconditioned gradient methods, covering, in the nonconvex case, full and diagonal AdaGrad, AdaNorm, Shampoo and Muon, with and without momentum, and without assuming boundedness of the gradients or a sufficiently small stepsize parameter.

  2. 2.

    It does so by considering a variable/parameter space structured as the product of blocks of potentially different types (much as in [54]) and by providing new simple proofs based on non-trivial trace inequalities and the theory of operator monotone functions. The present framework allows combining heterogeneous geometries across different blocks of a Cartesian product space, while preserving a unified complexity analysis and a globally consistent complexity. This is of special interest for adaptive methods because one may fear that the (possibly very) different adaptive stepsizes could generate strong distortions between the rates of convergence across blocks. Besides the obvious difference in proof techniques, it differs from the approach of [54] in that it does not require convexity of the objective function and covers the case where momentum is used.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the structured parameter space and our general algorithmic framework. Its convergence properties are established in Section 3, while Section 4 details why this framework covers full and diagonal AdaGrad, AdaNorm, Shampoo and Muon. Some conclusions and perspectives are finally outlined in Section 5.

Notations: In what follows, ∥⋅∥E\|\cdot\|_{E} denotes the Euclidean norm and the symbols ⪰\succeq and ⪯\preceq respectively denote the “larger or equal” and “less or equal” relations in the Löwner semi-order on positive semidefinite matrices. If ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is a norm on some space S{\pazocal{S}} endowed with an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle, its dual norm ∥⋅∥D\|\cdot\|_{D} is defined by ‖x‖∗=maxy∈S⁡⟨y,x⟩/‖y‖\|x\|_{*}=\max_{y\in{\pazocal{S}}}\langle y,x\rangle/\|y\|.

2 Parameter space structure and algorithmic framework

In order to exploit the possible different types of parameters occurring in problem (1.1), we separate them into LL disjoint blocks of uniform type (vectors or matrices), that is

X=(X1,…,XL),Xℓ∈IRnℓ×mℓ.X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{L}),\qquad X_{\ell}\in\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}}.

Thus each block contains dℓ=nℓ​mℓd_{\ell}=n_{\ell}m_{\ell} parameters, and the total number of parameters (the dimension of our complete optimization space) is

N=∑ℓ=1Lnℓ​mℓ=∑ℓ=1Ldℓ,N=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}n_{\ell}m_{\ell}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}, (2.1)

with dℓ=nℓ​mℓd_{\ell}=n_{\ell}m_{\ell}. We also define dmax=maxℓ∈{1,…,L}⁡dℓd_{\max}=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}}d_{\ell}. Each block ℓ\ell is equipped with a norm ∥⋅∥ℓ\|\cdot\|_{\ell} and its dual norm ∥⋅∥∗,ℓ\|\cdot\|_{*,\ell}. The canonical pairing in the Cartesian product space IRN=∏ℓ=1LIRdℓ\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{N}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{d_{\ell}} is then defined as

⟨U,V⟩=∑ℓ=1L⟨Uℓ,Vℓ⟩F, where ​⟨A,B⟩F=tr⁡(AT​B).\left\langle U,V\right\rangle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left\langle U_{\ell},V_{\ell}\right\rangle_{F},\;\;\mbox{ where }\;\;\left\langle A,B\right\rangle_{F}=\tr(A^{T}B).

The (primal) product space is endowed with the norm

‖D‖2=∑ℓ=1L‖Dℓ‖ℓ2,\|D\|^{2}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|D_{\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2},

whose dual norm is

‖Z‖∗2=∑ℓ=1L‖Zℓ‖∗,ℓ2.\|Z\|_{*}^{2}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|Z_{\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}. (2.2)

(Given a primal norm, the corresponding dual norm is the natural norm to measure gradients or their approximations. The use of dual norms for preconditioning has a long history (e.g. [12, Section 9.4]), and has emerged in the machine learning community following [19, 25, 9, 8, 5] or [41] for instance.)

In this context, our objective is to find a first-order critical point for problem (1.1), that is an X∗X_{*} such that

𝔼⁡[‖∇X1​f​(X∗,ξ)‖∗]=0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla_{X}^{1}f(X_{*},\xi)\|_{*}\right]=0.

In order to define our algorithmic framework to achieve this goal, we choose, for each block ℓ\ell, a measurable selector Sℓ​(⋅)S_{\ell}(\cdot) such that, for any DD,

Sℓ​(D)∈arg⁡max‖V‖ℓ≤1⁡⟨D,V⟩F,S_{\ell}(D)\in\arg\max_{\|V\|_{\ell}\leq 1}\left\langle D,V\right\rangle_{F},

which implies that

‖Sℓ​(D)‖ℓ={1if ​D≠00if ​D=0.\|S_{\ell}(D)\|_{\ell}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;D\neq 0\\ 0&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;D=0.\end{array}\right. (2.3)

(A similar definition was used in [25] for the single-block convex case.) For notational simplicity, the fact that Sℓ​(0)=0S_{\ell}(0)=0 is implicitly assumed in what follows. We also define an iteration-dependent linear operator Lk,ℓ​(D):IRnℓ×mℓ→IRnℓ×mℓ{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(D):\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}}\to\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}} by

Lk,ℓ​(D)2=defLk,ℓ​(D)∗​Lk,ℓ​(D).{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(D)^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(D)^{*}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(D). (2.4)

Since computing Gk=𝔼⁡[∇X1​f​(X∗,ξ)]G_{k}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{X}^{1}f(X_{*},\xi)\right] is in general either impossible or too expensive, we consider an iterative stochastic approach in which, at iterate XkX_{k}, GkG_{k} is approximated by an oracle G~k\widetilde{G}_{k} depending on a random variable ξk\xi_{k}, where ξk\xi_{k} (whose distribution may depend on XkX_{k}) is defined on some probability space (Ω,F,ℙ)(\Omega,{\pazocal{F}},\mathbb{P}) (𝔼\mathbb{E} denotes the corresponding expectation). The expectation conditioned to knowing (ξ0,…,ξk−1)(\xi_{0},\ldots,\xi_{k-1}) is denoted by the symbol 𝔼k​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\cdot\right].

Our simple but general algorithmic ADPREC framework is described 2.

This algorithm thus defines a random process (G~k,Zk,Γk,Xk)(\widetilde{G}_{k},Z_{k},\Gamma_{k},X_{k}), where G~k=(G~k,1,…,G~k,L)\widetilde{G}_{k}=(\widetilde{G}_{k,1},\ldots,\widetilde{G}_{k,L}), Zk=(Zk,1,…,Zk,L)Z_{k}=(Z_{k,1},\ldots,Z_{k,L}) and Γk=(Γk,1,…,Γk,L)\Gamma_{k}=(\Gamma_{k,1},\ldots,\Gamma_{k,L}). Immediately note that the choice G~k,ℓ=∇Xk,ℓ1​f​(Xk,ξk)\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}=\nabla_{X_{k,\ell}}^{1}f(X_{k},\xi_{k}) is possible, but, as we will see later, other choices are possible. At first sight, it may seem that the algorithm performs separate optimization on each block, but this view is deceptive because interaction between the blocks occurs in the computation of the approximate gradient. The name ADPREC alludes to the fact that Γk,ℓ\Gamma_{k,\ell} may be interpreted as an adaptive preconditioner for block ℓ\ell and (2.7) therefore produces an adaptively preconditioned (approximate) gradient Zk,ℓZ_{k,\ell}.

Note that (2.4) allows changing the update formula in (2.6) for Γk,ℓ\Gamma_{k,\ell} at each iteration although, as far as the authors know, this is not done in practice.

3 Convergence analysis

The convergence analysis for ADPREC hinges on the following standard assumptions.

Assumption 1 (Boundedness)

There exists a constant flowf_{\rm low} such that 𝔼⁡[f⁡(X,ξ)]≥flow\mathbb{E}\!\left[f(X,\xi)\right]\geq f_{\rm low} for all XX.

Assumption 2 (Smoothness)

The objective function ff is continuously differentiable and has a Lipschitz continuous gradient, that is there exists a constant LG≥0L_{G}\geq 0 such that, for all X,Y∈IRNX,Y\in\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{N}, ‖G⁡(X)−G⁡(Y)‖∗≤LG​‖X−Y‖.\|G(X)-G(Y)\|_{*}\leq L_{G}\|X-Y\|.

We now introduce conditions that define the class of instances of ADPREC for which we develop our theory. Although seemingly abstract, we will demonstrate in Section 4 that these conditions do hold for several popular first-order methods.

Assumption 3 (Structural identities)

For all k≥0k\geq 0 and all ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, we have that

∥Zk,ℓ∥∗,ℓ⟨G~k,ℓ,Sℓ(Zk,ℓ)⟩F=tr(Γk,ℓ−1/2Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2),\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}=\tr\!\big(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}\big), (3.1)

and

‖Zk,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2=tr⁡(Γk,ℓ−1​Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)2).\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}=\tr\!\big(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}\big). (3.2)

As will become clear in Lemma 3.1 just below, these identities reformulate the terms associated with first-order descent (for (3.1)) and second-order perturbations (for (3.2)) in terms of traces. Note that (3.1) and (3.2) are “iteration-specific” conditions, in that they only involve Γk,ℓ\Gamma_{k,\ell} and are independent of the value of Γk−1,ℓ\Gamma_{k-1,\ell}.

Assumption 4 (Gradient-preconditioner compatibility)

There exists a constant κ∘>0\kappa_{\circ}>0 such that, for each block ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, each k≥0k\geq 0 and all GℓG_{\ell},

‖G~ℓ‖∗,ℓ2≤κ∘​tr⁡(Lk,ℓ​(G~ℓ)2).\|\widetilde{G}_{\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\leq\kappa_{\circ}\,\tr\big({\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{\ell})^{2}\big). (3.3)

Because Lk,ℓ​(⋅){\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\cdot) is used to build the preconditioners Γk,ℓ\Gamma_{k,\ell}, this last assumption establishes the link between them and the measures of (approximate) optimality G~k,ℓ\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}. (Note that we could choose κ∘\kappa_{\circ} depending on ℓ\ell, but we use a single constant for simplicity.)

We of course need to be more specific on what we assume on the oracle G~k\widetilde{G}_{k}, but postpone the precise nature of our requirements to the statements of the results where they are needed.

Our first step is to analyze the (expected) descent at iteration kk.

Lemma 3.1
Suppose that Assumption 2 holds. Then 𝔼k​[f⁡(Xk+1)]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[f(X_{k+1})\right]\leq f⁡(Xk)−η​∑ℓ=1L𝔼k​[‖Zk,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​⟨G~k,ℓ,Sℓ​(Zk,ℓ)⟩F]\displaystyle f(X_{k})-\eta\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\right] (3.4) +η∑ℓ=1L𝔼k[∥Zk,ℓ∥∗,ℓ|⟨G~k,ℓ−Gk,ℓ,Sℓ(Zk,ℓ)⟩F|]+LG​η22∑ℓ=1L𝔼k[∥Zk,ℓ∥∗,ℓ2].\displaystyle+\eta\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\big|\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}-G_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\big|\right]+\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right].

  • Proof.    By Lipschitz continuity of the gradient (Assumption 2),

    f⁡(Xk+1)≤f⁡(Xk)+⟨Gk,Xk+1−Xk⟩+LG2​‖Xk+1−Xk‖2.f(X_{k+1})\leq f(X_{k})+\left\langle G_{k},X_{k+1}-X_{k}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{G}}{2}\|X_{k+1}-X_{k}\|^{2}.

    Thus, using (2.7) and (2.8), we obtain

    f⁡(Xk+1)≤f⁡(Xk)−η​∑ℓ=1L‖Zk,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​⟨Gk,ℓ,Sℓ​(Zk,ℓ)⟩F+LG​η22​∑ℓ=1L‖Zk,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2​‖Sℓ​(Zk,ℓ)‖ℓ2.f(X_{k+1})\leq f(X_{k})-\eta\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\left\langle G_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}+\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\|S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\|_{\ell}^{2}.

3.1 Trace inequalities

Our argument now takes a little linear algebra detour for proving two useful inequalities about the trace of matrices of interest. We first derive an inequality involving the trace of the inverse square root of the sum of two matrices.

Theorem 3.2
Let AA and BB be symmetric positive semidefinite matrices. Then tr((A+B)−1/2B)≥tr((A+B)1/2)−tr(A1/2).\tr\!\big((A+B)^{-1/2}B\big)\geq\tr((A+B)^{1/2})-\tr(A^{1/2}). (3.5)

  • Proof.    Set X=(A+B)1/2X=(A+B)^{1/2} and Y=A1/2Y=A^{1/2}. Clearly, X≻0X\succ 0, Y≻0Y\succ 0, and X+Y≻0X+Y\succ 0 and is therefore invertible. Moreover

    B=X2−Y2=X⁡(X−Y)+(X−Y)​Y.B=X^{2}-Y^{2}=X(X-Y)+(X-Y)Y. (3.6)

    Multiplying this inequality on the right by (X+Y)−1(X+Y)^{-1} gives

    B​(X+Y)−1=X⁡(X−Y)​(X+Y)−1+(X−Y)​Y​(X+Y)−1.B(X+Y)^{-1}=X(X-Y)(X+Y)^{-1}+(X-Y)Y(X+Y)^{-1}.

    Taking the trace and using cyclicity, we obtain that

    tr⁡(B​(X+Y)−1)\displaystyle\tr\!\big(B(X+Y)^{-1}\big) =tr⁡((X+Y)−1​X​(X−Y))+tr⁡((X+Y)−1​(X−Y)​Y)\displaystyle=\tr\!\big((X+Y)^{-1}X(X-Y)\big)+\tr\!\big((X+Y)^{-1}(X-Y)Y\big)
    =tr⁡((X+Y)−1​(X⁡(X−Y)+(X−Y)​Y))\displaystyle=\tr\!\Big((X+Y)^{-1}\big(X(X-Y)+(X-Y)Y\big)\Big)
    =tr⁡((X+Y)−1​((X−Y)​(X+Y)−[X,Y]))\displaystyle=\tr\!\Big((X+Y)^{-1}\big((X-Y)(X+Y)-[X,Y]\big)\Big)

    where [X,Y]=X​Y−Y​X[X,Y]=XY-YX is the commutator between XX and YY. Since XX and YY are Hermitian, [X,Y][X,Y] is skew-Hermitian and its trace is zero. Hence, using cyclicity (twice),

    tr⁡((X+Y)−1​B)=tr⁡(B​(X+Y)−1)\displaystyle\tr\!\big((X+Y)^{-1}B\big)=\tr\!\big(B(X+Y)^{-1}\big) =tr⁡((X+Y)−1​(X−Y)​(X+Y))−tr⁡((X+Y)−1​[X,Y])\displaystyle=\tr\!\big((X+Y)^{-1}(X-Y)(X+Y)\big)-\tr\!\big((X+Y)^{-1}[X,Y]\big)
    =tr⁡((X+Y)−1​(X−Y)​(X+Y))\displaystyle=\tr\!\big((X+Y)^{-1}(X-Y)(X+Y)\big)
    =tr⁡(X−Y)\displaystyle=\tr(X-Y)

    Now, since Y⪰0Y\succeq 0, we have that X+Y⪰XX+Y\succeq X. Since both XX and X+YX+Y are positive definite and since inversion reverses the Löwner semi-order, we deduce that

    (X+Y)−1⪯X−1=(A+B)−1/2.(X+Y)^{-1}\preceq X^{-1}=(A+B)^{-1/2}.

    and thus (A+B)−1/2−(X+Y)−1⪰0(A+B)^{-1/2}-(X+Y)^{-1}\succeq 0. But, since BB is symmetric positive definite, we deduce, again using cyclicity, that

    tr(((A+B)−1/2−(X+Y)−1)B)=tr(B1/2((A+B)−1/2−(X+Y)−1)B1/2)⪰0,\tr\!\Big(\big((A+B)^{-1/2}-(X+Y)^{-1}\big)B\Big)=\tr\!\Big(B^{1/2}\big((A+B)^{-1/2}-(X+Y)^{-1}\big)B^{1/2}\Big)\succeq 0,

    and therefore that

    tr((A+B)1/2)−tr(A1/2)=tr(X−Y)=tr((X+Y)−1B)≤tr((A+B)−1/2B),\tr\!\Big((A+B)^{1/2}\Big)-\tr\!\Big(A^{1/2}\Big)=\tr(X-Y)=\tr\!\Big((X+Y)^{-1}B\Big)\leq\tr\!\Big((A+B)^{-1/2}B\Big),

    which is (3.5). □\Box

The next step of our argument uses the Löwner semi-order ⪰\succeq on symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices and the theory of operator monotone functions (see [10, Chapter V], for instance).

Theorem 3.3
Let AA and BB be symmetric positive semidefinite matrices and let ϕ:(0,∞)→ℝ\phi:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be a C1C^{1} function. Suppose that ϕ′\phi^{\prime} is operator monotone decreasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty), meaning that for any positive definite matrices X,YX,Y, X⪯Y​implies that​ϕ′​(X)⪰ϕ′​(Y).X\preceq Y\;\;\mbox{implies that}\;\;\phi^{\prime}(X)\succeq\phi^{\prime}(Y). Then tr⁡(ϕ′​(A+B)​B)≤tr⁡(ϕ⁡(A+B)−ϕ⁡(A))≤tr⁡(ϕ′​(A)​B).\tr\!\big(\phi^{\prime}(A+B)B\big)\leq\tr\!\big(\phi(A+B)-\phi(A)\big)\leq\tr\!\big(\phi^{\prime}(A)B\big). (3.7)

  • Proof.    Define g⁡(t)=deftr⁡(ϕ⁡(A+t​B))g(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\tr\!\big(\phi(A+tB)\big) for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Using the standard derivative formula for spectral functions under the trace, we see that

    g′​(t)=tr⁡(ϕ′​(A+t​B)​B).g^{\prime}(t)=\tr\!\big(\phi^{\prime}(A+tB)B\big). (3.8)

    Since B⪰0B\succeq 0, we also have that

    A⪯A+t​B⪯A+B(t∈[0,1]).A\preceq A+tB\preceq A+B\qquad(t\in[0,1]). (3.9)

    and hence, because ϕ′\phi^{\prime} is operator monotone decreasing, that

    ϕ′​(A+B)⪯ϕ′​(A+t​B)⪯ϕ′​(A).\phi^{\prime}(A+B)\preceq\phi^{\prime}(A+tB)\preceq\phi^{\prime}(A).

    Now if M⪯NM\preceq N and B⪰0B\succeq 0, then tr⁡((N−M)​B)=tr⁡(B1/2​(N−M)​B1/2)≥0\tr((N-M)B)=\tr(B^{1/2}(N-M)B^{1/2})\geq 0, and thus tr⁡(M​B)≤tr⁡(N​B)\tr(MB)\leq\tr(NB). Using this inequality in (3.9) and the identity (3.8), we therefore obtain that

    tr⁡(ϕ′​(A+B)​B)≤g′​(t)≤tr⁡(ϕ′​(A)​B).\tr\!\big(\phi^{\prime}(A+B)B\big)\leq g^{\prime}(t)\leq\tr\!\big(\phi^{\prime}(A)B\big).

    Integrating over t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] then yields (3.7). □\Box

We now use the above and a classical result by K. Löwner to deduce two helpful inequalities on the trace of matrices generated by the ADPREC algorithm.

Lemma 3.4
We have that, for all k≥0k\geq 0, ∑ℓ=1Ltr(Γk,ℓ1/2)−∑ℓ=1Ltr(Γ−1,ℓ1/2)≤∑j=0k∑ℓ=1Ltr(Γj,ℓ−1/2Lk,ℓ(G~j,ℓ)2)\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{-1,\ell}^{1/2})\leq\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr\!\left(\Gamma_{j,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell})^{2}\right) (3.10) and ∑j=0k∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γj,ℓ−1​Lk,ℓ​(G~j,ℓ)2)≤∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(log⁡(Γk,ℓ))−∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(log⁡(Γ−1,ℓ)).\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr\!\left(\Gamma_{j,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell})^{2}\right)\leq\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr\!\Big(\log(\Gamma_{k,\ell})\Big)-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr\!\Big(\log(\Gamma_{-1,\ell})\Big). (3.11)

  • Proof.    Let

    A=Γj−1,ℓ​ and ​B=Lj,ℓ​(G~j,ℓ)2.A=\Gamma_{j-1,\ell}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;B={\pazocal{L}}_{j,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell})^{2}. (3.12)

    Then Γj,ℓ=A+B\Gamma_{j,\ell}=A+B and Theorem 3.2 gives that, for j∈{0,…,k}j\in\{0,\ldots,k\} and ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\},

    tr(Γj,ℓ1/2)−tr(Γj−1,ℓ1/2)≤tr(Γj,ℓ−1/2Lj,ℓ(G~j,ℓ)2).\tr(\Gamma_{j,\ell}^{1/2})-\tr(\Gamma_{j-1,\ell}^{1/2})\leq\tr\!\Big(\Gamma_{j,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{j,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell})^{2}\Big).

    Summing this inequality for j∈{0,…,k}j\in\{0,\ldots,k\} and ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\} yields (3.10). In order to prove (3.11), let ϕ⁡(t)=log⁡t\phi(t)=\log t. Then ϕ′​(t)=1t.\phi^{\prime}(t)=\frac{1}{t}. which is operator monotone decreasing (see [37] as cited in [10, p. 149]). Applying the first inequality of (3.7) in Theorem 3.3 then yields that

    tr⁡((A+B)−1​B)≤tr⁡(log⁡(A+B)−log⁡A),\tr\!\Big((A+B)^{-1}B\Big)\leq\tr\!\Big(\log(A+B)-\log A\Big),

    which, with (3.12), ensures that, for j∈{0,…,k}j\in\{0,\ldots,k\} and ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\},

    tr⁡(Γj,ℓ−1​Lj,ℓ​(G~j,ℓ)2)≤tr⁡(log⁡(Γj,ℓ))−tr⁡(log⁡(Γj−1,ℓ)).\tr\!\Big(\Gamma_{j,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{j,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell})^{2}\Big)\leq\tr\!\Big(\log(\Gamma_{j,\ell})\Big)-\tr\!\Big(\log(\Gamma_{j-1,\ell})\Big).

    Summing this inequality for j∈{0,…,k}j\in\{0,\ldots,k\} and ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\} now yields (3.11). □\Box

3.2 Telescoping inequality and global rate of convergence

We next introduce a variant of the classical telescoping argument, leading to the central inequality in our analysis.

Theorem 3.5
Suppose that Assumption 1 and 3 hold. Suppose also that, for some ω≥0\omega\geq 0 and νk≥0\nu_{k}\geq 0 ∑j=0k𝔼⁡[‖G~j−Gj‖∗2]≤νk2+ω2​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2].\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j}-G_{j}\|_{*}^{2}\right]\leq\nu_{k}^{2}+\omega^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]. (3.13) Define Δk=def𝔼⁡[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(log⁡Γk,ℓ)−∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(log⁡Γ−1,ℓ)].\Delta_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\log\Gamma_{k,\ell})-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\log\Gamma_{-1,\ell})\right]. (3.14) Then, for every k≥0k\geq 0, η​𝔼​[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)]≤κgap+η​νk​Δk+(η​ω2+LG​η22)​Δk,\eta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right]\leq\kappa_{\mbox{\tiny gap}}+\eta\,\nu_{k}\,\sqrt{\Delta_{k}}+\left(\eta\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\right)\,\Delta_{k}, (3.15) where κgap=def𝔼⁡[f⁡(X0)]−flow+η​ς​∑ℓ=1Ldℓ.\kappa_{\mbox{\tiny gap}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[f(X_{0})\right]-f_{\rm low}+\eta\,\varsigma\,\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}. (3.16)

  • Proof.    Taking the full expectation in the conditional descent inequality (3.4) and summing for j=0j=0 to kk gives

    η∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L\displaystyle\eta\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L} 𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​⟨G~j,ℓ,Sℓ​(Zj,ℓ)⟩F]≤𝔼⁡[f⁡(X0)]−flow\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[f(X_{0})\right]-f_{\rm low} (3.17)
    +η∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼[∥Zj,ℓ∥∗,ℓ|⟨G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ,Sℓ(Zj,ℓ)⟩F|]+LG​η22∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼[∥Zj,ℓ∥∗,ℓ2∥Sℓ(Zj,ℓ)∥ℓ2].\displaystyle+\eta\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\big|\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\big|\right]+\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\|S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\|_{\ell}^{2}\right].

    Using successively (3.1) and (3.10), we obtain that

    η​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​⟨G~j,ℓ,Sℓ​(Zj,ℓ)⟩F]\displaystyle\eta\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\right] =η∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼[tr(Γj,ℓ−1/2Lj,ℓ(G~j,ℓ)2)]\displaystyle=\eta\,\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tr\!\bigl(\Gamma_{j,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{j,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell})^{2}\bigr)\right] (3.18)
    ≥η​𝔼​[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)−∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γ−1,ℓ1/2)].\displaystyle\geq\eta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{-1,\ell}^{1/2})\right].

    Now observe that the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and (2.3) give that

    |⟨G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ,Sℓ​(zj,ℓ)⟩F|≤‖G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​‖Sℓ​(Zj,ℓ)‖ℓ≤‖G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ.\big|\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\big|\leq\|\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\|S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\|_{\ell}\leq\|\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}.

    Therefore

    𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​|⟨G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ,Sℓ​(Zj,ℓ)⟩F|]≤𝔼⁡[‖G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2]​𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\big|\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\big|\right]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]}\,\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]}.

    Observe now that the Cauchy-Scwartz inequality also implies that, for any vectors aa and bb with nonnegative components,

    ∑jaj​bj≤‖a‖E​‖b‖E=∑jaj​∑jbj.\sum_{j}\sqrt{a_{j}}\sqrt{b_{j}}\leq\|\sqrt{a}\|_{E}\,\|\sqrt{b}\|_{E}=\sqrt{\sum_{j}a_{j}}\sqrt{\sum_{j} b_{j}}. (3.19)

    Hence, summing over ℓ\ell and using (2.2), we obtain that

    ∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​|⟨G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ,Sℓ​(Zj,ℓ)⟩F|]≤𝔼⁡[‖G~j−Gj‖∗2]​∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2].\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\big|\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\big|\right]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j}-G_{j}\|_{*}^{2}\right]}\,\sqrt{\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]}.

    Summing now over jj and using (3.19) again, we deduce that

    η∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L\displaystyle\eta\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L} 𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​|⟨G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ,Sℓ​(zj,ℓ)⟩F|]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\big|\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\big|\right]
    ≤η​∑j=0k𝔼⁡[‖G~j−Gj‖∗2]​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2]\displaystyle\leq\eta\,\sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j}-G_{j}\|_{*}^{2}\right]}\,\sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]}
    ≤η​νk​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2]+η​ω2​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2]\displaystyle\leq\eta\nu_{k}\sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]}+\eta\omega^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]

    where we used (3.13) to obtain the last inequality. But, by (3.2), (3.11) and (3.14),

    ∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2]=∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[tr⁡(Γj,ℓ−1​Lj,ℓ​(G~j,ℓ)2)]≤Δk,\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tr\!\bigl(\Gamma_{j,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{j,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell})^{2}\bigr)\right]\leq\Delta_{k}, (3.20)

    so that

    η​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ​|⟨G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ,Sℓ​(Zj,ℓ)⟩F|]≤η​νk​Δk+η​ω2​Δk.\eta\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\big|\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}\big|\right]\leq\eta\,\nu_{k}\,\sqrt{\Delta_{k}}+\eta\omega^{2}\Delta_{k}. (3.21)

    Similarly, using (2.3) and (3.20), the quadratic term satisfies

    LG​η22​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2​‖Sℓ​(Zj,ℓ)‖ℓ2]=LG​η22​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖Zj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2]≤LG​η22​Δk.\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\|S_{\ell}(Z_{j,\ell})\|_{\ell}^{2}\right]=\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|Z_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\Delta_{k}. (3.22)

    Substituting (3.18), (3.21) and (3.22) into (3.17) then yields that

    η​𝔼​[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)−∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γ−1,ℓ1/2)]≤f⁡(X0)−flow+η​νk​Δk+(η​ω2+LG​η22)​Δk,\eta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{-1,\ell}^{1/2})\right]\leq f(X_{0})-f_{\rm low}+\eta\,\nu_{k}\,\sqrt{\Delta_{k}}+\left(\eta\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\right)\Delta_{k}, (3.23)

    which is exactly (3.15)-(3.16) after taking into account that Γ−1,ℓ=ς​Iℓ\Gamma_{-1,\ell}=\varsigma I_{\ell} for all ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}. □\Box

We now start exploiting this result by deriving a more specific bound on the value of Δk\Delta_{k} in (3.14). This requires the following simple technical lemma.

Lemma 3.6
Let Γ∈IRd×d\Gamma\in\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{d\times d} be symmetric positive definite. Then tr⁡(log⁡Γ)≤2​d​log⁡(tr⁡(Γ1/2))−d​log⁡(d).\tr(\log\Gamma)\leq 2d\log\!\bigl(\tr(\Gamma^{1/2})\bigr)-d\log(d).

  • Proof.    Let λ1,…,λd>0\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d}>0 be the eigenvalues of Γ\Gamma. Then the concavity of the logarithm ensures that

    tr⁡(log⁡Γ)=∑i=1dlog⁡(λi)≤d​log⁡(1d​∑i=1dλi)≤d​log⁡((∑i=1dλi)2d)=2​d​log⁡(tr⁡(Γ1/2))−d​log⁡(d).\tr(\log\Gamma)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log(\lambda_{i})\leq d\log\!\left(\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}\right)\leq d\log\!\left(\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}\right)^{2}}{d}\right)=2d\log\!\bigl(\tr(\Gamma^{1/2})\bigr)-d\log(d).

    □\Box

We now derive the desired bound on Δk\Delta_{k} in (3.14).

Lemma 3.7
We have that, for all k≥0k\geq 0, Δk≤κ0+2​N​log⁡(𝔼⁡[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)]),\Delta_{k}\leq\kappa_{0}+2N\log\!\left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right]\right), (3.24) where κ0=−∑ℓ=1Ldℓlog(dℓ)−log(ς)N.\kappa_{0}=-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}\log(d_{\ell})-\log(\varsigma)N. (3.25)

  • Proof.    Applying Lemma 3.6 to each block gives

    ∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(log⁡Γk,ℓ)≤2​∑ℓ=1Ldℓ​log⁡(tr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2))−∑ℓ=1Ldℓ​log​dℓ.\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\log\Gamma_{k,\ell})\leq 2\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}\log\!\bigl(\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\bigr)-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}\log d_{\ell}. (3.26)

    Since tr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)≤∑r=1Ltr⁡(Γk,r1/2),\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\leq\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,r}^{1/2}), we have that log⁡(tr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2))≤log⁡(∑r=1Ltr⁡(Γk,r1/2)),\log\!\bigl(\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\bigr)\leq\log\!\left(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,r}^{1/2})\right), and hence, from (3.26),

    ∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(log⁡Γk,ℓ)≤2​∑ℓ=1Ldℓ​log⁡(∑r=1Ltr⁡(Γk,r1/2))−∑ℓ=1Ldℓ​log​dℓ.\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\log\Gamma_{k,\ell})\leq 2\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}\log\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,r}^{1/2})\right)-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}\log d_{\ell}.

    We therefore obtain from (3.14) that

    Δk≤−∑ℓ=1Ldℓlogdℓ−∑ℓ=1Ltr(logΓ−1,ℓ)+2∑ℓ=1Ldℓ𝔼[log(∑ℓ=1Ltr(Γk,ℓ1/2))].\Delta_{k}\leq-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}\log d_{\ell}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\log\Gamma_{-1,\ell})+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right)\right]. (3.27)

    But Jensen’s inequality for the concave log⁡(⋅)\log(\cdot) function gives that

    𝔼⁡[log⁡(∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2))]≤log⁡(𝔼⁡[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)]).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right)\right]\leq\log\!\left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right]\right).

    Inserting this inequality in (3.27) and using the definition Γ−1,ℓ=ς​Iℓ\Gamma_{-1,\ell}=\varsigma I_{\ell} gives (3.24)-(3.25). □\Box

We still need a simple technical result before concluding.

Lemma 3.8
Suppose that 1≤t≤c​log⁡(t)1\leq t\leq c\log(t) for c≥0c\geq 0 and t≥1t\geq 1. Then t≤2​c​log⁡(2​c)t\leq 2c\log(2c).

  • Proof.   Lemma 3.2 in [6] with a=1a=1 and b=0b=0 gives that t≤2​c​(log⁡(2​c)−1)t\leq 2c\Big(\log(2c)-1\Big). □\Box

We now state a first important result on the expected size of the preconditioners Γk,ℓ\Gamma_{k,\ell}.

Theorem 3.9
Suppose that the ADPREC algorithm is applied to problem (1.1). Suppose that (3.13) and Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold. Then, for all k≥0k\geq 0, 𝔼⁡[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)]≤Θk=defmax⁡[emax⁡[1,12​N,κ02​N],3​κgapη,Tk,Yk],\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right]\leq\Theta_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\max\left[\,e^{\max\left[1,\frac{1}{2N},\frac{\kappa_{0}}{2N}\right]},\,\frac{3\kappa_{\mbox{\tiny gap}}}{\eta},T_{k},Y_{k}\,\right], (3.28) with κgap\kappa_{\mbox{\tiny gap}} defined in (3.16), Tk=12​N​νk​max⁡[1,log⁡(12​N​νk)],Yk=24​N​(ω2+LGη)​log⁡(24​N​(ω2+LGη))T_{k}=12\sqrt{N}\,\nu_{k}\,\sqrt{\max\left[1,\log\left(12\sqrt{N}\,\nu_{k}\right)\right]},\;\;\;\;Y_{k}=24N\left(\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}}{\eta}\right)\log\left(24N\left(\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}}{\eta}\right)\right) νk\nu_{k} being defined in (3.13) and κ0\kappa_{0} in (3.25).

  • Proof.    Define

    tk=𝔼⁡[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)].t_{k}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right]. (3.29)

    Substituting (3.24) into (3.15) and using this definition then gives that

    η​tk≤κgap+η​νk​κ0+2​N​log⁡(tk)+(η​ω2+LG​η22)​(κ0+2​N​log⁡(tk)).\eta\,t_{k}\leq\kappa_{\rm gap}+\eta\,\nu_{k}\,\sqrt{\kappa_{0}+2N\log\left(t_{k}\right)}+\left(\eta\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}\eta^{2}}{2}\right)\bigl(\kappa_{0}+2N\log\left(t_{k}\right)\bigr). (3.30)

    Suppose first that

    log⁡(tk)<max⁡[12​N,κ02​N].\log\left(t_{k}\right)<\max\left[\frac{1}{2N},\frac{\kappa_{0}}{2N}\right].

    Then

    tk≤emax⁡[12​N,κ02​N].t_{k}\leq e^{\max\left[\frac{1}{2N},\frac{\kappa_{0}}{2N}\right]}. (3.31)

    Alternatively, suppose now that

    2​N​log⁡(tk)≥max⁡[1,κ0].2N\log\left(t_{k}\right)\geq\max[1,\kappa_{0}]. (3.32)

    Then

    κ0+2​N​log⁡(tk)≤4​N​log⁡(tk)\kappa_{0}+2N\log\left(t_{k}\right)\leq 4N\log\left(t_{k}\right)

    and (3.30) can then be rewritten as

    tk≤a+b​νk​log⁡(tk)+c​log⁡(tk)t_{k}\leq a+b\,\nu_{k}\sqrt{\log(t_{k})}+c\log(t_{k}) (3.33)

    with

    a=κgapη,b=2​N​ and ​c=4​N​(ω2+LGη).a=\frac{\kappa_{\mbox{\tiny gap}}}{\eta},\;\;\;\;b=2\sqrt{N}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;c=4N\left(\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}}{\eta}\right). (3.34)

    This formulation is analyzed by distinguishing three cases.
    ∙\bullet The first case is when max⁡[a,b​νk​log⁡(tk),c​log⁡(tk)]=a\max[a,b\nu_{k}\sqrt{\log(t_{k})},c\log(t_{k})]=a. Then, clearly,

    tk≤3​a.t_{k}\leq 3a. (3.35)

    ∙\bullet The second case is when

    If log⁡(tk)≤1\log(t_{k})\leq 1, then tk≤et_{k}\leq e. Alternatively, if log⁡(tk)>1\log(t_{k})>1 (implying that tk>1t_{k}>1), we deduce that tk2≤9​b2​νk2​log⁡(tk),t_{k}^{2}\leq 9b^{2}\nu_{k}^{2}\log(t_{k}), that is

This result finally gives us all the ingredients to derive convergence and complexity results on the Cartesian product space. The bound (3.28), together with Assumption 4, indeed implies convergence of the criticality measure on each block with a uniform rate-of-convergence bound.

Theorem 3.10
Suppose that the ADPREC algorithm is applied to problem (1.1). Suppose that (3.13) and Assumptions 1 to 4 hold. Then ∑j=0k𝔼⁡[‖G~j‖∗]≤k+1​κ∘​Θk\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j}\|_{*}\right]\leq\sqrt{k+1}\,\kappa_{\circ}\,\Theta_{k} (3.41) where Θk\Theta_{k} is defined in Theorem 3.9. Moreover, if G~k\widetilde{G}_{k} is an unbiased estimator of GkG_{k}, i.e. 𝔼k​[G~k]=Gk\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\widetilde{G}_{k}\right]=G_{k} for all k≥0k\geq 0, then minj∈{0,…,k}⁡𝔼⁡[‖Gj‖∗]≤1k+1​∑j=0k𝔼⁡[‖Gj‖∗]≤κ∘​Θkk+1.\min_{j\in\{0,\ldots,k\}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{j}\|_{*}\right]\leq\frac{1}{k+1}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{j}\|_{*}\right]\leq\frac{\kappa_{\circ}\,\Theta_{k}}{\sqrt{k+1}}. (3.42)

  • Proof.    Assumption 4 and Theorem 3.9 directly imply that

    ∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼⁡[‖G~j,ℓ‖∗,ℓ]≤k+1​κ∘​∑j=0k𝔼⁡[∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(Γk,ℓ1/2)]≤k+1​κ∘​Θk.\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\right]\leq\sqrt{k+1}\,\kappa_{\circ}\,\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{1/2})\right]\leq\sqrt{k+1}\,\kappa_{\circ}\,\Theta_{k}.

    Dividing by k+1k+1 and using 𝔼k​[G~k]=Gk\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\widetilde{G}_{k}\right]=G_{k} together with Jensen’s inequality gives (3.42). □\Box

Observe that the requirement (3.13) defines an upper bound on νk\nu_{k}, the cumulative total variance of the gradient oracle over all past iterates, an approach more general than assuming conditional variance at every iteration. In particular, it allows large variance at early iterations provided later iterations compensate. Trade-offs between different realizations are also theoretically possible. Also note that, since we prove that Γk\Gamma_{k} grows very slowly (see (3.28)), and ZkZ_{k} is the preconditioned approximate gradient, condition (3.13) is akin to a cumulative affine variance condition of the form

∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼j​[‖G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ‖2]≤νk2+ω2​∑j=0k∑ℓ=1L𝔼j​[‖Gj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2],\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{j}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell}\|^{2}\right]\leq\nu_{k}^{2}+\omega^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{j}\!\left[\|G_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right],

whose iteration-wise variant has already been used in analysis of first-order methods (see [18, 49] or, for the stronger “ affine-∗ ” version, [4]). In particular, the “strong growth” assumption motivated by over-parametrized problems and used in [49] to derive an improved convergence rate for AdaGrad is essentially subsumed (at the cumulative level) if “preconditioned cumulative strong growth” (that is νk=0\nu_{k}=0 is assumed in (3.13)).

We now investigate what can be said if one makes a more specific assumption on conditional variance at each iteration.

Although the rates of convergence obtained in Corollary 3.11 under the bias and variance conditions (3.43) are reasonable, they do not quite match, for high-variance regimes, the best obtained so far for (momentum-less) AdaGrad and AdaNorm [49]. However they recover (in order) the best O⁡(log⁡(k+1)​log⁡(log⁡(k+1))/(k+1)){\pazocal{O}}(\sqrt{\log(k+1)\log(\log(k+1))/(k+1)}) rate in the preconditioned cumulative strong growth context22 2 That is not only in the case where σℓ=0\sigma_{\ell}=0 for each ℓ\ell, but, more generally, in the case where the “inaccuracy budget” νk2\nu_{k}^{2} is finite.. Importantly, they do so for a large class of algorithms. We however note that, should the restrictive assumption of a bounded gradient oracle be made for AdaGrad, only the first part of (3.43) (unbiased oracle) is necessary to deduce that the average of 𝔼⁡[‖Gk‖E2]\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{k}\|_{E}^{2}\right] decreases like O⁡(1/(k+1)1/4){\pazocal{O}}(1/(k+1)^{1/4}) [21], thereby allowing arbitrary variance.

3.3 Adding momentum (twice)

Because of its widespread use, we now consider properties of variants of ADPREC augmented with momentum. Suppose now that, for some 0≤μk≤μmax<10\leq\mu_{k}\leq\mu_{\max}<1, all k≥0k\geq 0 and ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, (2.7) and (2.6) are replaced by

Mk,ℓ\displaystyle M_{k,\ell} =\displaystyle= μk​Mk−1,ℓ+(1−μk)​G~k,ℓ,\displaystyle\mu_{k}M_{k-1,\ell}+(1-\mu_{k})\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}, (3.45)
Γk,ℓ\displaystyle\Gamma_{k,\ell} =\displaystyle= Γk−1,ℓ+Lk,ℓ​(Mk,ℓ)2,\displaystyle\Gamma_{k-1,\ell}+{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(M_{k,\ell})^{2}, (3.46)
Zk,ℓ\displaystyle Z_{k,\ell} =\displaystyle= Γk,ℓ−1/2Mk,ℓ\displaystyle\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}M_{k,\ell} (3.47)

where we have defined, for all ℓ\ell, M−1,ℓ=G~0,ℓM_{-1,\ell}=\widetilde{G}_{0,\ell} so that M0,ℓ=G~0,ℓM_{0,\ell}=\widetilde{G}_{0,\ell}. This modification of the algorithm in effect adds a specific type of momentum, although this is not the only possible one. Another variant where Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ){\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}) is used instead of Lk,ℓ​(Mk,ℓ){\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(M_{k,\ell}) will be considered at the end of this section.

We now show that the theory of the previous section can be extended to cover this case. We start by establishing a bound on the norm of the difference between the block-wise momentum Mk,ℓM_{k,\ell} and the approximate gradient G~k,ℓ\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}, which we now define as G~k,ℓ=∇Xℓ1​f​(Xk,ξk)\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}=\nabla_{X_{\ell}}^{1}f(X_{k},\xi_{k}).

We now wish to apply the theory above by considering that the momentum Mk,ℓM_{k,\ell} plays the role of the approximate gradient (in Step 1 of ADPREC) in this theory. In particular, this change of perspectives implies that Assumption 3 now becomes

Assumption 5 (Modified structural identities)

For all k≥0k\geq 0 and all ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, we have that

∥Zk,ℓ∥∗,ℓ⟨Mk,ℓ,Sℓ(Zk,ℓ)⟩F=tr(Γk,ℓ−1/2Lk,ℓ(Mk,ℓ)2),\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}\,\left\langle M_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle_{F}=\tr\!\big(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(M_{k,\ell})^{2}\big), (3.51)

and

‖Zk,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2=tr⁡(Γk,ℓ−1​Lk,ℓ​(Mk,ℓ)2).\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}=\tr\!\big(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(M_{k,\ell})^{2}\big). (3.52)

Fortunately, using our theory is possible because, as we show below, (3.49) implies that condition (3.13) of Theorem 3.5 holds with suitable constants. This allows us to derive the analog of Theorem 3.10 for the “momentum” variant of ADPREC.

    But the definition of Θk\Theta_{k} in (3.28) gives that νk≤Θk\nu_{k}\leq\Theta_{k}, and (3.53) then follows by dividing by k+1k+1 and using a+b≤a+b\sqrt{a+b}\leq\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}. □\Box

The difference between (3.42) and (3.53) is only a constant and a logarithmic term in factor of (k+1)−1/2(k+1)^{-1/2}. As a consequence, the global rate of convergence of the momentum variant of ADPREC is essentially identical to that of the version without momentum, and Corollary 3.11 still applies to the momentum variant.

We finally note that our momentum definition and convergence analysis do not make the assumption that the stepsize parameter η\eta is sufficiently small, in contrast with previous proofs of convergence where results assume that η\eta is small enough, in particular smaller than a multiple of the (usually unknown) Lipschitz constant LGL_{G} [23, 26, 53].

The momentum approach we have described above uses (3.45)–(3.47). Another version could be considered, using (3.45) and (3.47) but keeping the “pure gradient” technique (2.6) to accumulate the preconditioner, that is

Γk,ℓ\displaystyle\Gamma_{k,\ell} =\displaystyle= Γk−1,ℓ+Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)2,\displaystyle\Gamma_{k-1,\ell}+{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}, (3.58)
Mk,ℓ\displaystyle M_{k,\ell} =\displaystyle= μk​Mk−1,ℓ+(1−μk)​G~k,ℓ,\displaystyle\mu_{k}M_{k-1,\ell}+(1-\mu_{k})\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}, (3.59)
Zk,ℓ\displaystyle Z_{k,\ell} =\displaystyle= Γk,ℓ−1/2Mk,ℓ.\displaystyle\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}M_{k,\ell}. (3.60)

As it turns out, it is also possible to derive a unified convergence theory for this choice, albeit this requires stronger assumptions and leads to a worse rate of convergence if μk\mu_{k} is kept bounded away from zero. However, selecting the sequence {μk}\{\mu_{k}\} adequately allows recovering the rate of the momentum-less variant. This alternative theory hinges on the fact that Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ){\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}) can be viewed as a perturbation of Lk,ℓ​(Mk,ℓ){\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(M_{k,\ell}) , and therefore that the structural relations of Assumption 5 are themselves perturbed. Fortunately, it remains possible to bound these perturbations by a mix of variance-related and second-order terms, the first of which potentially affecting the resulting global convergence rate. The final outcome is given by the following theorem and corollary (whose detailed proofs can be found in appendix).

Theorem 3.14
Suppose that the ADPREC algorithm with (2.7) replaced by (3.59) and (3.60) is applied to problem (1.1). Suppose that Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5 hold. If μ>0\mu>0, suppose also that there exists constants κ□,κ⋄>0\kappa_{\Box},\kappa_{\diamond}>0 such that Lk,ℓ​(U+V)2⪯κ□​Lk,ℓ​(U)2+κ□​Lk,ℓ​(V)2​ and ​tr⁡(Lk,ℓ​(U)2)≤κ⋄​‖U‖∗,ℓ2{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(U+V)^{2}\preceq\kappa_{\Box}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(U)^{2}+\kappa_{\Box}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(V)^{2}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\tr\!\Big({\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(U)^{2}\Big)\leq\kappa_{\diamond}\|U\|_{*,\ell}^{2} (3.61) for all ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, k≥0k\geq 0 and all U,V∈IRnℓ×mℓU,V\in\hbox{I\hskip-2.0ptR}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}}, and that either ​η≤1−μmaxμmax​LG​ς6​κ□​κ⋄​ or ​∑j=0∞μj2​‖Zj‖∗2≤κμ​Z\;\;\mbox{either }\;\;\eta\leq\frac{1-\mu_{\max}}{\mu_{\max}\,L_{G}}\sqrt{\frac{\varsigma}{6\kappa_{\Box}\kappa_{\diamond}}}\;\;\mbox{ ~or~ }\;\;\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\mu_{j}^{2}\|Z_{j}\|_{*}^{2}\leq\kappa_{\mu Z} (3.62) for some κμ​Z≥0\kappa_{\mu Z}\geq 0. Then ∑j=0k𝔼⁡[‖G~j‖∗]≤k+1​κ∘​Θk\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j}\|_{*}\right]\leq\sqrt{k+1}\,\kappa_{\circ}\,\Theta_{k} (3.63) where Θk=max⁡[emax⁡[1,12​N,κ02​N],3​(κgap+κν​ν​θk2)η,Tk,Yk],\Theta_{k}=\max\left[\,e^{\max\left[1,\frac{1}{2N},\frac{\kappa_{0}}{2N}\right]},\,\frac{3(\kappa_{\mbox{\tiny gap}}+\kappa_{\nu\nu}\theta_{k}^{2})}{\eta},T_{k},\,Y_{k}\,\right], (3.64) with θk2=∑j=0k∑ℓ=1Lμj2​𝔼​[‖G~j,ℓ−Gj,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2],Tk=12​N​κν​Δ​θk​max⁡[1,log⁡(12​N​κν​Δ​θk)],\theta_{k}^{2}=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mu_{j}^{2}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{j,\ell}-G_{j,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}\right],\;\;\;\;T_{k}=12\sqrt{N}\,\kappa_{\nu\Delta}\,\theta_{k}\,\sqrt{\max\left[1,\log\left(12\sqrt{N}\,\kappa_{\nu\Delta}\,\theta_{k}\right)\right]}, (3.65) Yk=24​N​κΔ​(ω2+LGη)​log⁡(24​N​κΔ​(ω2+LGη))Y_{k}=24N\kappa_{\Delta}\left(\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}}{\eta}\right)\log\left(24N\kappa_{\Delta}\left(\omega^{2}+\frac{L_{G}}{\eta}\right)\right) κ∘\kappa_{\circ} being defined in Assumption 4, κ0\kappa_{0} in (3.25), and κgap\kappa_{\mbox{\tiny gap}}, κν​ν\kappa_{\nu\nu}, κν​Δ\kappa_{\nu\Delta} and κΔ\kappa_{\Delta} in (A.13)–(A.14). Moreover, if G~k\widetilde{G}_{k} is an unbiased estimator of GkG_{k}, i.e. 𝔼k​[G~k]=Gk\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\widetilde{G}_{k}\right]=G_{k} for all k≥0k\geq 0, then minj∈{0,…,k}⁡𝔼⁡[‖Gj‖∗]≤1k+1​∑j=0k𝔼⁡[‖Gj‖∗]≤κ∘​Θkk+1.\min_{j\in\{0,\ldots,k\}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{j}\|_{*}\right]\leq\frac{1}{k+1}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{j}\|_{*}\right]\leq\frac{\kappa_{\circ}\,\Theta_{k}}{\sqrt{k+1}}. (3.66)

As it turns out, assuming (3.61) is not restrictive in the applications considered in this paper, as we briefly discuss below in appendix. Supposing (3.62) is definitely less desirable because the value of the Lipschitz constant LGL_{G} or that of κμ​Z\kappa_{\mu Z} (if it exists) is usually unknown. It is however common practice in the literature [23, 26, 53]. Note the term κν​ν​νk2\kappa_{\nu\nu}\nu_{k}^{2} in the middle term of (3.64), which is the crucial difference between (3.64) and (3.28) and that induces the modified convergence rate expressed by the following corollary.

Corollary 3.15
Suppose that the ADPREC algorithm with (2.7) replaced by (3.59) and (3.60) is applied to problem (1.1). Suppose that Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5 hold. If μ>0\mu>0, suppose also that (3.61) and (3.62) hold, that 𝔼k​[G~k]=Gk​ and ​𝔼k​[‖G~k,ℓ−Gk,ℓ‖∗2]≤σℓ2(k+1)α\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\widetilde{G}_{k}\right]=G_{k}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\left[\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}-G_{k,\ell}\|_{*}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{\sigma_{\ell}^{2}}{(k+1)^{\alpha}} (3.67) for some α>0\alpha>0 and all k≥0k\geq 0 and ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, and that μk=μmax(k+1)β\mu_{k}=\frac{\mu_{\max}}{(k+1)^{\beta}} for some μmax<1\mu_{\max}<1 and some β≥0\beta\geq 0. Then 1k+1​∑j=0k𝔼⁡[‖Gj‖∗]={O⁡(1(k+1)α+2​β−12)if ​α+2​β<1,O⁡(log⁡(k+1)​log⁡(log⁡(k+1))k+1)if ​α+2​β=1,O⁡(1k+1)if ​α+2​β>1.\frac{1}{k+1}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{j}\|_{*}\right]=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\pazocal{O}}\left(\frac{\displaystyle 1}{\displaystyle(k+1)^{\alpha+2\beta-{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}}}\right)&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\alpha+2\beta<1,\\ {\pazocal{O}}\left(\frac{\displaystyle\sqrt{\log(k+1)\log(\log(k+1))}}{\displaystyle\sqrt{k+1}}\right)&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\alpha+2\beta=1,\\ {\pazocal{O}}\left(\frac{\displaystyle 1}{\displaystyle\sqrt{k+1}}\right)&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\alpha+2\beta>1.\end{array}\right.

Again, be aware that the constants hidden in the O⁡(⋅){\pazocal{O}}(\cdot) depend on α\alpha, preventing taking limits for α\alpha tending to one. The rate of convergence now depends on the value of α+2​β\alpha+2\beta, indicating how acting on the momentum parameter μk\mu_{k} can alleviate the effect of a high gradient-oracle variance. Because the convergence rate is, in this case, determined by νk\nu_{k} as defined in (3.65), choosing a small momentum parameter in effect reduces the propagation of larger errors in the gradient oracle across iterations. In particular, setting μk\mu_{k} to a multiple of k−14​αk^{-{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{4}}\alpha} recovers the rate of the momentum-less variant also for the high-variance regime (α<1\alpha<1). If however μk\mu_{k} is kept constant (or bounded away from zero), that is if β=0\beta=0, then (3.67) is stronger than (3.43) and the rate of convergence for α<1\alpha<1 is now O⁡((k+1)12−α){\pazocal{O}}\left((k+1)^{{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}-\alpha}\right) instead of O⁡((k+1)−α2){\pazocal{O}}\left((k+1)^{-{\scriptstyle\frac{\alpha}{2}}}\right), requiring in particular that α>12\alpha>{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}.

One should however be careful not to identify better theoretical convergence properties with better practical performance on specific classes of problems. Indeed, limited numerical experiments suggest that the second momentum variant might outperform the first.

4 Application to existing algorithms

We now consider four popular first-order algorithms and show that their convergence behaviour is covered by the above results by considering a single block (L=1L=1). But, we also show that this is also true if they are applied blockwise in a more complex setting. This is achieved by clarifying the correspondence between ADPREC and each algorithm and verifying that (3.1), (3.2) and (3.3) hold in each case for all blocks concerned. In all cases considered here, the preconditioner update Lk,ℓ{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell} is independent of kk. For simplicity of exposition, we focus on the situation where there is no momentum (μk=0\mu_{k}=0). We also use lower case symbols for vectors.

4.1 AdaNorm [45, 15, 51]

Taking the AdaNorm update on a given block ℓ\ell, corresponds to choosing an isotropic scalar geometry. More specifically, if block ℓ\ell has dimension nℓn_{\ell}, one considers

Γ−1,ℓ=ς​Inℓ​ and ​Γk,ℓ=Γk−1,ℓ+‖g~k,ℓ‖ℓ2nℓ​Inℓ(k≥0),\Gamma_{-1,\ell}=\varsigma I_{n_{\ell}}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\Gamma_{k,\ell}=\Gamma_{k-1,\ell}+\frac{\|\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2}}{n_{\ell}}I_{n_{\ell}}\;\;\;\;(k\geq 0),

so that the contribution of this block to the step is

sk,ℓ=−ηΓk,ℓ−1/2g~k,ℓ=−ηγk,ℓg~k,ℓs_{k,\ell}=-\eta\,\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}=-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\gamma_{k,\ell}}}\,\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}

when Γk,ℓ=γk,ℓ​Inℓ\Gamma_{k,\ell}=\gamma_{k,\ell}I_{n_{\ell}}. This is exactly the AdaNorm update on block ℓ\ell.

In ADPREC, this corresponds to choosing

mℓ=1,∥⋅∥∗,ℓ=∥⋅∥ℓ,Sℓ(G~k,ℓ)=G~k,ℓ‖G~k,ℓ‖ℓ, and Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2=‖G~k,ℓ‖ℓ2nℓInℓ.m_{\ell}=1,\qquad\|\cdot\|_{*,\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{\ell},\qquad S_{\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})=\frac{\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}}{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}},\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}=\frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2}}{n_{\ell}}I_{n_{\ell}}. (4.1)

With these choices, we have that

Zk,ℓ=Γk,ℓ−1/2G~k,ℓ and tr(Γk,ℓ−1Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2)=tr(‖G~k,ℓ‖ℓ2nℓΓk,ℓ−1).Z_{k,\ell}=\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\tr\left(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}\right)=\tr\left(\frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2}}{n_{\ell}}\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}\right).

If Γk,ℓ=γk,ℓ​Inℓ\Gamma_{k,\ell}=\gamma_{k,\ell}I_{n_{\ell}}, this becomes

tr⁡(Γk,ℓ−1​Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)2)=‖G~k,ℓ‖ℓ2γk,ℓ=‖Zk,ℓ‖ℓ2,\tr\left(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}\right)=\frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2}}{\gamma_{k,\ell}}=\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2},

which is (3.2). Similarly,

tr(Γk,ℓ−1/2Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2)=‖G~k,ℓ‖ℓ2γk,ℓ=∥Zk,ℓ∥ℓ⟨G~k,ℓ,Sℓ(Zk,ℓ)⟩,\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2})=\frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2}}{\sqrt{\gamma_{k,\ell}}}=\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{\ell}\,\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle,

proving (3.1). Moreover, Assumption 4 also holds on block ℓ\ell. Indeed, for any G~ℓ\widetilde{G}_{\ell}, the second and last parts of (4.1) give

tr⁡(Lk,ℓ​(G~ℓ)2)=‖G~ℓ‖ℓ2=‖G~ℓ‖∗,ℓ2,\tr({\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{\ell})^{2})=\|\widetilde{G}_{\ell}\|_{\ell}^{2}=\|\widetilde{G}_{\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2},

and thus (3.3) holds with κ∘=1\kappa_{\circ}=1.

Thus, whenever a block ℓ\ell is endowed with this isotropic scalar geometry, Theorem 3.10 and Corollary 3.11 apply to that block without modification. The standard “one block” AdaNorm is obtained when there is only one block (L=1,n1=d1=N)(L=1,n_{1}=d_{1}=N).

4.2 Full AdaGrad [15]

Taking the “full” version of AdaGrad [15] update on block ℓ\ell corresponds to choosing, on a given block ℓ\ell, a full matrix-valued geometry. More precisely, if block ℓ\ell has dimension nℓn_{\ell}, one considers

Γ−1,ℓ=ς​Inℓ​ and ​Γk,ℓ=Γk−1,ℓ+g~k,ℓ​g~k,ℓT(k≥0),\Gamma_{-1,\ell}=\varsigma I_{n_{\ell}}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\Gamma_{k,\ell}=\Gamma_{k-1,\ell}+\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}^{T}\;\;\;\;(k\geq 0),

so that the contribution of this block to the step is sk,ℓ=−ηΓk,ℓ−1/2g~k,ℓ.s_{k,\ell}=-\eta\,\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}. This is exactly the full AdaGrad update on block ℓ\ell.

In ADPREC, this corresponds to choosing

mℓ=nℓ,∥⋅∥∗,ℓ=∥⋅∥ℓ=∥⋅∥E,Sℓ(G~k,ℓ)=G~k,ℓ/∥G~k,ℓ∥E, and Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2=G~k,ℓG~k,ℓT.m_{\ell}=n_{\ell},\qquad\|\cdot\|_{*,\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{E},\qquad S_{\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})=\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}/\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{E},\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}=\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}^{T}. (4.2)

With these choices, we have that

Zk,ℓ=Γk,ℓ−1/2G~k,ℓ, and tr(Γk,ℓ−1Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2)=tr(Γk,ℓ−1/2G~k,ℓG~k,ℓTΓk,ℓ−1/2)=∥Zk,ℓ∥E2,Z_{k,\ell}=\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2})=\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}^{T}\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2})=\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{E}^{2},

which is (3.2). Similarly,

tr(Γk,ℓ−1/2Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2)=tr(Γk,ℓ−1/2G~k,ℓG~k,ℓT)=⟨G~k,ℓ,Zk,ℓ⟩=∥Zk,ℓ∥E⟨G~k,ℓ,Sℓ(Zk,ℓ)⟩,\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2})=\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}^{T})=\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},Z_{k,\ell}\right\rangle=\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{E}\,\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle,

proving (3.1). Moreover, Assumption 4 also holds on block ℓ\ell. Indeed, for any GℓG_{\ell}, the second and last part of (4.2) give

tr⁡(Lk,ℓ​(G~ℓ)2)=tr⁡(G~ℓ​G~ℓT)=‖G~ℓ‖E2=‖G~ℓ‖∗,ℓ\tr({\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{\ell})^{2})=\tr(\widetilde{G}_{\ell}\widetilde{G}_{\ell}^{T})=\|\widetilde{G}_{\ell}\|_{E}^{2}=\|\widetilde{G}_{\ell}\|_{*,\ell}

so that (3.3) holds with c∘=1c_{\circ}=1.

Thus, whenever a block ℓ\ell is endowed with this full matrix geometry, Theorem 3.10, and Corollary 3.11 apply to that block without modification.

4.3 Diagonal AdaGrad [15, 39]

We now turn to the use of the diagonal/component-wise AdaGrad update on a given block ℓ\ell. If block ℓ\ell has dimension nℓn_{\ell}, this geometry is defined by

Γ−1,ℓ=ςInℓ and Γk,ℓ=Γk−1,ℓ+Diag((g~k,ℓ)i2)(k≥0) and xk+1,ℓ=xk,ℓ−ηΓk,ℓ−1/2g~k,ℓ.\Gamma_{-1,\ell}=\varsigma I_{n_{\ell}}\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\Gamma_{k,\ell}=\Gamma_{k-1,\ell}+\mathrm{Diag}\big((\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell})_{i}^{2}\big)\;\;\;\;(k\geq 0)\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;x_{k+1,\ell}=x_{k,\ell}-\eta\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}.

In our framework, this corresponds to choosing

mℓ=nℓ,∥⋅∥∗,ℓ=∥⋅∥ℓ=∥⋅∥E,Lk,ℓ(g~k,ℓ)=Diag(|(g~k,ℓ)i|), and Sℓ(g~k,ℓ)=g~k,ℓ/∥g~k,ℓ∥E,m_{\ell}=n_{\ell},\qquad\|\cdot\|_{*,\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{E},\qquad{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell})=\mathrm{Diag}\big(|(\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell})_{i}|\big),\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;S_{\ell}(\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell})=\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}/\|\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}\|_{E}, (4.3)

so that

Lk,ℓ​(g~k,ℓ)2=Diag⁡((g~k,ℓ)i2).{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell})^{2}=\mathrm{Diag}\big((\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell})_{i}^{2}\big).

We then have that

Zk,ℓ=Γk,ℓ−1/2G~k,ℓ, and tr(Γk,ℓ−1Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2)=∑i=1nℓ(G~k,ℓ)i2(Γk,ℓ)i​i=∥Zk,ℓ∥E2,Z_{k,\ell}=\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\ell}}\frac{(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})_{i}^{2}}{(\Gamma_{k,\ell})_{ii}}=\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{E}^{2},

which proves (3.2). Moreover,

tr(Γk,ℓ−1/2Lk,ℓ(G~k,ℓ)2)=∑i=1nℓ(G~k,ℓ)i2(Γk,ℓ)i​i=⟨G~k,ℓ,Zk,ℓ⟩=∥Zk,ℓ∥E⟨G~k,ℓ,Sℓ(Zk,ℓ)⟩,\tr(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\ell}}\frac{(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})_{i}^{2}}{\sqrt{(\Gamma_{k,\ell})_{ii}}}=\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},Z_{k,\ell}\right\rangle=\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{E}\,\left\langle\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},S_{\ell}(Z_{k,\ell})\right\rangle,

which proves (3.1). Moreover, Assumption 4 also holds in this case. Indeed, for any Gℓ∈ℝnℓG_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}},

Lk,ℓ​(Gℓ)=Diag⁡(|(Gℓ)i|),Lk,ℓ​(Gℓ)2=Diag⁡((Gℓ)i2),{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(G_{\ell})=\mathrm{Diag}\big(|(G_{\ell})_{i}|\big),\qquad{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(G_{\ell})^{2}=\mathrm{Diag}\big((G_{\ell})_{i}^{2}\big),

and therefore

tr⁡(Lk,ℓ​(Gℓ)2)=∑i=1nℓ(Gℓ)i2=‖Gℓ‖E2=‖Gℓ‖∗,ℓ2,\tr({\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(G_{\ell})^{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\ell}}(G_{\ell})_{i}^{2}=\|G_{\ell}\|_{E}^{2}=\|G_{\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2},

so that (3.3) holds with κ∘=1\kappa_{\circ}=1.

Thus, as above, Theorem 3.10 and Corollary 3.11 apply without modification to this diagonal AdaGrad geometry on block ℓ\ell.

Observe that we could also view the diagonal AdaGrad algorithm as a Cartesian product of scalar AdaNorm. Also note that, as discussed in Section 3.3, momentum in the form (3.45)-(3.47) or (3.58)-(3.60) may be introduced on this block, resulting in an ADPREC variant somewhat similar to Adam [30]. It is theoretically interesting that this variant enjoys the convergence behaviour described by Theorem 3.13 and Corollary 3.11, in contrast with Adam.

4.4 Adaptive Shampoo [25]

Shampoo [25] is a stochastic preconditioned optimization method designed for tensor parameters and in particular matrix blocks in neural networks. We consider here an adaptive variant of this algorithm. We assume a block structure with LL blocks, each associated with matrix parameter Xk,ℓ∈ℝnℓ×mℓX_{k,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}}, implying that dℓ=nℓ​mℓd_{\ell}=n_{\ell}m_{\ell}. Given a stochastic gradient G~k,ℓ\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}, the Adaptive Shampoo algorithm maintains the Gram matrices

Lk,ℓ=Lk−1,ℓ+G~k,ℓ​G~k,ℓT,Rk,ℓ=Rk−1,ℓ+G~k,ℓT​G~k,ℓ,L_{k,\ell}=L_{k-1,\ell}+\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}^{T},\qquad R_{k,\ell}=R_{k-1,\ell}+\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}^{T}\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell},

initialized with L−1,ℓ=R−1,ℓ=ς​IL_{-1,\ell}=R_{-1,\ell}=\varsigma I. The Shampoo preconditioned gradient is

We now express Shampoo in the framework of ADPREC. On ℝnℓ×mℓ\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}}, we choose

∥⋅∥ℓ=∥⋅∥F,∥⋅∥∗,ℓ=∥⋅∥F,Sℓ(Z)=Z/∥Z∥F.\|\cdot\|_{\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{F},\qquad\|\cdot\|_{*,\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{F},\qquad S_{\ell}(Z)=Z/\|Z\|_{F}.

Let g~k,ℓ=vec⁡(G~k,ℓ)\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}=\operatorname{vec}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}) and zk,ℓ=vec⁡(Zk,ℓ).z_{k,\ell}=\operatorname{vec}(Z_{k,\ell}). Using vec⁡(A​M​B)=(BT⊗A)​vec⁡(M)\operatorname{vec}(AMB)=(B^{T}\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(M), we obtain that

vec(Z^k,ℓ)=(Rk,ℓ−1/4⊗Lk,ℓ−1/4)g~k,ℓ.\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{Z}_{k,\ell})=(R_{k,\ell}^{-1/4}\otimes L_{k,\ell}^{-1/4})\,\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}. (4.5)

Define

Γk,ℓ−1/2=Rk,ℓ−1/4⊗Lk,ℓ−1/4,Γk,ℓ=Rk,ℓ1/2⊗Lk,ℓ1/2.\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}=R_{k,\ell}^{-1/4}\otimes L_{k,\ell}^{-1/4},\qquad\Gamma_{k,\ell}=R_{k,\ell}^{1/2}\otimes L_{k,\ell}^{1/2}.

Then zk,ℓ=Γk,ℓ−1/2g~k,ℓ,z_{k,\ell}=\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1/2}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}, and thus Zk,ℓ=Z^k,ℓZ_{k,\ell}=\widehat{Z}_{k,\ell}. The ADPREC update becomes

Xk+1,ℓ=Xk,ℓ−η​Zk,ℓ,X_{k+1,\ell}=X_{k,\ell}-\eta Z_{k,\ell},

and choosing η=ηshampoo/dℓ\eta=\eta_{\rm shampoo}/\sqrt{d_{\ell}} recovers (4.4). We now define

Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)2=g~k,ℓ​g~k,ℓT,so thatLk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)2=g~k,ℓ​g~k,ℓT.{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}=\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}^{T},\qquad\text{so that}\qquad{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}=\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}^{T}.

Then

‖Zk,ℓ‖∗,ℓ2=‖zk,ℓ‖22=g~k,ℓT​Γk,ℓ−1​g~k,ℓ=tr⁡(Γk,ℓ−1​Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)2),\|Z_{k,\ell}\|_{*,\ell}^{2}=\|z_{k,\ell}\|_{2}^{2}=\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}^{T}\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}\widetilde{g}_{k,\ell}=\tr\!\left(\Gamma_{k,\ell}^{-1}{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}\right),

4.5 Adaptive MUON/AdaGO [28, 44, 56]

We now consider an AdaGrad-inspired adaptive version of MUON [28], as described as AdaGO for the single block case in [56]. In our framework, this corresponds to assigning, for each block ℓ\ell, a geometry adapted to the structure of neural network parameters. We distinguish two types of blocks. For ℓ∈M\ell\in{\pazocal{M}}, Gk,ℓG_{k,\ell} is a matrix of size nℓ×mℓn_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}, while for ℓ∈A={1,…,L}∖M\ell\in{\pazocal{A}}=\{1,\ldots,L\}\setminus{\pazocal{M}}, Gk,ℓG_{k,\ell} is a vector in ℝnℓ\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}}. For ℓ∈A\ell\in{\pazocal{A}}, we use

∥⋅∥ℓ=∥⋅∥E=∥⋅∥∗,ℓ,\|\cdot\|_{\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{E}=\|\cdot\|_{*,\ell},

while for ℓ∈M\ell\in{\pazocal{M}},

∥⋅∥ℓ=∥⋅∥s,∥⋅∥∗,ℓ=∥⋅∥∗.\|\cdot\|_{\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{s},\qquad\|\cdot\|_{*,\ell}=\|\cdot\|_{*}.

The MUON normalization is defined by

Sℓ​(G~k,ℓ)={Uk,ℓ​Vk,ℓTif ​ℓ∈M​and​G~k,ℓ=Uk,ℓ​Σk,ℓ​Vk,ℓT,G~k,ℓ/‖G~k,ℓ‖Eif ​ℓ∈A.S_{\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}U_{k,\ell}V_{k,\ell}^{T}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{M}}\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}=U_{k,\ell}\Sigma_{k,\ell}V_{k,\ell}^{T},\\ \widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}/\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{E}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{A}}.\end{array}\right.

We then define, for each block ℓ\ell,

Γk,ℓ=γk,ℓ​Idℓ, where ​γ−1,ℓ=ς​ and ​γk,ℓ={γk−1,ℓ+‖G~k,ℓ‖∗2/dℓif ​ℓ∈M,γk−1,ℓ+‖G~k,ℓ‖E2/dℓif ​ℓ∈A.\Gamma_{k,\ell}=\gamma_{k,\ell}\,I_{d_{\ell}},\;\;\mbox{ where }\;\;\gamma_{-1,\ell}=\varsigma\;\;\mbox{ and }\;\;\gamma_{k,\ell}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\gamma_{k-1,\ell}+\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{*}^{2}/d_{\ell}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{M}},\\ \gamma_{k-1,\ell}+\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{E}^{2}/d_{\ell}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{A}}.\end{array}\right. (4.6)

This corresponds to choosing, for each block ℓ\ell,

Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)={‖G~k,ℓ‖∗dℓ​Idℓif ​ℓ∈M,‖G~k,ℓ‖Edℓ​Idℓif ​ℓ∈A,​ so that ​Lk,ℓ​(G~k,ℓ)2={‖G~k,ℓ‖∗2dℓ​Idℓif ​ℓ∈M,‖G~k,ℓ‖E2dℓ​Idℓif ​ℓ∈A.{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{*}}{\sqrt{d_{\ell}}}I_{d_{\ell}}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{M}},\\ \frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{E}}{\sqrt{d_{\ell}}}I_{d_{\ell}}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{A}},\end{array}\right.\;\;\mbox{ so that }\;\;{\pazocal{L}}_{k,\ell}(\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell})^{2}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{*}^{2}}{d_{\ell}}I_{d_{\ell}}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{M}},\\ \frac{\|\widetilde{G}_{k,\ell}\|_{E}^{2}}{d_{\ell}}I_{d_{\ell}}&\;\;\mbox{if }\;\;\ell\in{\pazocal{A}}.\end{array}\right.

With these choices, the ADPREC algorithm corresponds to a block-wise adaptive MUON method, with stepsize ηmuon,ℓ=η/dℓ\eta_{\rm muon,\ell}=\eta/\sqrt{d_{\ell}}. For ℓ∈A\ell\in{\pazocal{A}}, the verification of (3.1), (3.2) and (3.3) is identical to that of AdaNorm. For ℓ∈M\ell\in{\pazocal{M}}, we have

Thus (3.3) holds with κ∘=1\kappa_{\circ}=1 for all ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}. Therefore Theorem 3.10 and Corollary 3.11 apply without modification to this adaptive MUON geometry.

5 Conclusions

We have provided a general framework for first-order optimization algorithms using adaptively preconditioned gradients but no function values. We have shown that this framework covers a few of the popular adaptive first-order methods, including AdaGrad, full AdaGrad, AdaNorm, Shampoo and Muon, as well as any Cartesian mix of these. We have provided a fully stochastic rate-of-convergence analysis for all methods in the framework, with and without momentum, using standard assumptions on the variance of the gradient oracle and without assuming bounded stochastic gradients or small enough stepsizes.

Our results open several theoretical research issues. We anticipate that, as is the case for AdaGrad, the framework can be adapted to handle bounds [6] or more general convex [25, 13, 1] or nonconvex [16, 7, 22, 50] constraints, as well as second-order information (should it be available), but this requires verifications that are beyond the scope of the present paper. Other questions also remain. Is approximate normalization (i.e. approximate Sℓ​(⋅)S_{\ell}(\cdot)) acceptable? Can the generality of (2.4) be exploited to derive new preconditioners? Does the Cartesian framework allow more general algorithmic settings? Can the freedom to choose a different preconditioner update at each iteration be used to advantage? All these topics are the subject of ongoing investigation.
